{"number":768,"title":"Migration plan: baselining → versioned updates (engine/pack split)","body":"Rollout plan for the versioned-updates design (`docs/versioned-updates/DESIGN.md`, PR #767). Each phase is independently landable and leaves the fleet working.

**All phases are merged and the whole fleet runs the versioned flows.** Closed by #823; the defects the rollout surfaced are tracked separately under "Still open".

## Phase 0 — Version scaffolding — landed in #769
- [x] Engine version, stamped into the mount by the vendor set.
- [x] A version number on each canon pack's manifest.
- [x] `min_engine_version` in the schema, shape-validated. *(landed as `minEngineVersion`)*
- [x] Member stamp records installed engine version and per-pack versions.
- [x] Each migration record moved into its owning flow's home.
- [x] `escalation()`'s fired code made countable across the fleet.

## Phase 1 — Engine releases and the engine update flow — complete
- [x] Define an engine release. *(the **bump commit**, canary-gated — #776; engine 2 in #781, engine 3 in #791)*
- [x] Build the engine updater. *(#779)*
- [x] Version-gate migration fetching + rework `migrationActive()`. *(#778)*
- [x] Gate auto-merge on `selftest --strict`; red → PR open + `needs-human`. *(#782)*
- [x] `force-merge-on-red-ci`, per-invocation only. *(#782)*
- [x] Define the **custom update** lane. *(#782)*
- [x] Move the `local-pack-namespace` rewrite into a real engine migration. *(#781)*
- [x] Enforce no `agentic:` on an engine migration in the registry validator. *(#785)*

## Phase 2 — Pack update flow — complete
- [x] Build the pack updater. *(#782)*
- [x] **Converge `.github/workflows/`.** *(#797, in #791 — see the correction below; this was ticked in #782 and was not true)*
- [x] Version-gate per-pack migration fetching. *(#778 + #782)*
- [x] Enforce `min_engine_version` before apply, against the version the TARGET runs. *(#782)*
- [x] Uniform terminals for every non-green end. *(#782 — `updates/terminals.mjs`)*
- [x] Re-home the executor-routine verification into the apply stage. *(#782, then moved out of the retired brief into `tasks/update/task.md` in #791)*
- [x] **Implement the agentic apply stage.** *(#791 — dispatched, and verified end to end on the canary: staged → dispatch issue → executor routine → session moved the file and merged its own PR, with no intervention)*
- [x] Decide the apply stage from the RECORDS, not the version plan. *(#798, in #791)*

## Phase 3 — Install — complete
- [x] Install = the pack updater from a blank slate, **running no migrations**, stamping the latest version. *(#782)*
- [x] Route the adoption interview through the open-PR + `needs-human` terminal. *(#782)*
- [x] Run-once-at-install seed ops. *(#782)*
- [x] Give the install runner a CLI, and stamp the `requires` closure. *(#809)*
- [x] Converge **`adopt-pack`** onto the runner. *(#809)*
- [x] Converge **`adopt-claudinite`**. *(#823 — and not onto the runner, which turned out to be the wrong target; see the correction below)*

## Phase 4 — Cutover — complete (#785)
- [x] Convert the remaining `agentic:` notes.
  - [x] `pack-independence` — retired as drained (#782).
  - [x] `prework-rename` — retired (#785).
  - [x] `fleet-baseline-task` (sheepdog) — its note went with the field itself in Phase 5.
- [x] Switch stamp authority from the date to installed versions; retire the held-stamp gating. *(#785)*

## Phase 5 — Retirement — complete (#791)
- [x] Remove `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/`, its escalation codes, and its dispatch protocol.
- [x] Delete the `migrations/apply.mjs` + `migrations/registry.mjs` compatibility entry points.
- [x] Drop the `agentic:` field from the migration schema. *(rejected at load, not merely ignored)*
- [x] Vocabulary sweep: *baseline/baselining/rebaselining* → *update*.

## Phase 6 — Naming and the first real record — complete (#809)
- [x] Rename `maintenance.mechanism` `updates` → `versioned`, ending the one-letter collision with the `update` task.
- [x] Ship it as the **first record to declare `applyStage`** — a real instance, not a demonstration.
- [x] First `basics` version bump (1 → 2), which is what makes that record reachable at all.

## The rollout, as it actually went
**The whole fleet runs the versioned flows** — 14 repos: the canary plus 13 members (EdFringeNow, Sheepdog, MissingBulbWebsite, TLDR, ShoutsAndWhispers, LaughCounter, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, ClaudiniteWebsite, CrosswordChat, VascularColoring, HelloWorldFlutterApp, gRatio, EdFringeAllocator). Engine 3 is delivered; the scheduler wiring converged on all ten active members, CrosswordChat last and by hand (see below).

## Corrections this rollout forced
Recorded because each was believed and ticked before it was true.

- **The canary rehearsal gate was vacuous for weeks.** It drove the canary's *vendored baselining* worker, which correctly stood down and exited 0 in zero seconds. Every release qualified after the canary flipped was qualified by nothing. Fixed in #791: it now drives the worker the ref ships and fails without a convergence marker.
- **"The pack updater converges `.github/workflows/`" was ticked and false.** Nothing converged member wiring from the flip until #797. Members' scheduler workflows were frozen at whatever baselining last wrote — including the forced-run concurrency group, without which a fleet-wide `FORCE_TASKS` fan-out can be silently eaten.
- **Removing a flow-side export wedges the fleet.** #791 deleted `applyStageBrief` as dead code; every fielded worker calls it, and workers load flows from a *fresh canon clone*, so canon-side code goes current instantly while the calling worker stays a cycle stale. Fixed in #802, with a test pinning the surface fielded workers call. **The canary rehearsal cannot catch this class** — it runs the worker *this ref ships*, by design.
- **`update` is a daily task, not hourly.** The fleet would have taken two days to self-heal, parked at `apply-stage` throughout — not the hour I first claimed.
- **The stated reason for the install runner was wrong** (#809 → corrected in #823). `apply-vendor-set` was said to leave packs *unversioned*; it does not — it writes `packVersions` for every declared pack. The real hazard is the opposite and worse: it stamps them all at the **newest** version without running the records in between, and since `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, every skipped record stops applying *permanently*. Correct at version zero (which is why bootstrap still uses it), stranding anywhere else. So the last Phase 3 box was not "point `adopt-claudinite` at the runner" — it was that the skill told sessions to **refresh live members** this way. A refresh is now the update flow's job, not a session's.
- **The apply stage is not reliable end to end.** It ran unattended on the canary, and on the first real fleet cycle CrosswordChat's session claimed the dispatch and died without a commit. The stale-claim backstop escalated it correctly; nothing recovered it. Converged by hand.

## Still open
- **#803** — every escalated dispatch starts two executor sessions (GitHub emits a `labeled` event per label); one burns a container to read labels and stand down. The claim protocol correctly resolves it — this is cost and noise, not a race. Observed live on CrosswordChat #182, two claims four seconds apart.
- **#821** — a `needs-human` dispatch issue does not await triage, it *stops* its task: the at-most-one-open guard is `family.find((i) => i.state === 'open')`, label-blind. Found by fleet sweep: 13 tasks stopped this way across 9 repos, the oldest since 2026-07-23.
- **#822** — the fleet executor's repo allowlist is missing ClaudiniteCanary, so `canon-curation/growth-promote` cannot satisfy its binding Context.
- Retire `updates` from `MECHANISMS`. **Blocked on the three dormant members** (HelloWorldFlutterApp, gRatio, EdFringeAllocator): they still declare `mechanism: "updates"`, carry no `packVersions` at all, and their schedulers are stopped, so no record ever reaches them. Removing the legacy spelling hard-fails all three on wake.
- Retire the `applyStageBrief` shim once no fielded worker calls it. A test expires at engine 5 to force the decision.
- A record's `materialize` into `.github/workflows/` (#649's original case) shares the withhold path but has still never run live; only the scheduler-workflow route is exercised.

## What the flows share (settled while building)
- A record declares `version` — the owning flow's version its change takes effect at — and lands with that bump. Which flow owns it is structural.
- A record's `version` must be **≤ its pack's manifest version**, and the manifest must move for the record to reach an up-to-date member.

{"number":649,"title":"A migration cannot materialize a workflow file — baselining's push can never write .github/workflows/","body":"**Closed by the staging lane in #797 (PR #791), verified live on the canary.**

The original problem: a migration record could declare a `materialize` op whose `dest` is under `.github/workflows/`, and no flow could deliver it — the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there, and the refusal rejects the whole ref, so writing one would fail the entire converge rather than just that file. The stopgap was to skip such a materialization with a note.

Two things changed.

**The withhold is now real.** `updates/pack-update.mjs` routes every write bound for `.github/workflows/` to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, a path the Action token *can* push, and ends the update at `apply-stage` until a session with an MCP credential moves it into place. Same route for a record's materialization and for the scheduler workflow's own convergence — "a record materialized one" and "the file drifted" reach the apply stage as one list.

Worth recording that the announcement predated the mechanism: the pack flow already set `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS: '1'`, so `applyMaterializations` would have *written* the workflow file, `git add -A` would have staged it, and the push would have taken the whole cycle down. Latent only because no record has yet declared such a materialization — the first one would have failed every member's update. That is now closed too.

**Verified, not assumed.** On the canary: staged into the PR as an added file with `.github/workflows/` untouched; delivered by moving it byte for byte (the push succeeded, confirming a session credential reaches where the Action token cannot); and the next forced cycle reported `nothing changed — no branch, no PR`, with the staging directory swept. The lane opens and closes.

Reopen if a record's materialization behaves differently from the scheduler-workflow path — both go through the same `write`, but only the latter has been exercised against a live member.

# The LIVE CANARY (#593 phase 3) — the required final step of any core change.
#
# The fixture rehearsal (packs-tests/rehearsal/) is the fast gate: hermetic,
# seconds, on every PR. It has one honest weakness — a fixture only tests what
# someone remembered to model. This is the other half: a REAL repo, really
# adopting Claudinite, really running its own scheduler, converged against this
# canon ref and asked whether it still works.
#
# WHY IT IS A SEPARATE WORKFLOW. It takes minutes, needs a cross-repo token, and
# mutates another repository's working tree. A gate with those properties cannot
# run on every push without becoming something people route around. So: manual
# dispatch, plus automatic on merge to main — the post-merge smoke test, which
# the owner's own framing settles as "still much much better than not knowing".
#
# WHERE THE CANARY IS NAMED. In `.claudinite-checks.json`, on the `local/claudinite`
# pack entry's `config.canaryRepo` — the same tracked pack-entry config mechanism
# the sheepdog pack uses for its fleet scope. NOT a GitHub repository variable: the
# binding between this canon and its canary is a fact about the project, and a
# repository variable is invisible in the tree, absent from every diff, and cannot
# be reviewed alongside the workflow that acts on it. A reader of this repo should
# be able to see which repo CI is about to rewrite.
#
# WHY A DEDICATED REPO, NOT A REAL PROJECT. A rehearsal rewrites the mount and
# can leave a failed converge behind. Pointing that at EdFringeNow means a bad
# canon commit leaves a real project dirty at the exact moment attention is
# elsewhere. The canary is disposable by construction; that is its whole value.
#
# WHAT PROTECTS THE CANARY ITSELF: the worker's rehearsal mode
# (CLAUDINITE_CANON_REF) converges, reports, and then RESTORES the working tree —
# no commit, no branch, no PR, and above all no stamp. Stamping a branch head
# would leave the canary `ref-not-on-trunk`, which vendoring's #328 anti-rewind
# guard then refuses to converge over: a rehearsal that wedges its own canary.
name: Canary rehearsal

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Canon ref to rehearse (blank = this workflow's own ref)"
        required: false
        type: string
  push:
    branches: [main]
    # Only the surfaces a consumer actually vendors. A README or a doc change
    # cannot break a member, and spending minutes proving that teaches everyone
    # to ignore the result.
    paths:
      - 'engine/**'
      - 'packs/**'
      - 'vendoring/**'

permissions:
  contents: read

# The rehearse step pipes into tee, and GitHub's implicit `bash -e` has no
# pipefail — a worker exiting non-zero into a successful tee would show green.
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

concurrency:
  # One canary at a time: two rehearsals converging the same repo would race on
  # its working tree and report each other's damage.
  group: canary-rehearsal
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  rehearse:
    name: Rehearse against the canary repo
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - name: Check out the canon (for the declaration)
        uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Resolve the canary repo from the declaration
        id: cfg
        run: |
          CANARY=$(node -e '
            const c = require("./.claudinite-checks.json");

# Fleet baseline — force every member to baseline now

**This task runs no agent, and no schedule.** It is `frequency: manual` with `agent_model: none`: it never fires on any cadence, and the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) → [`force-fleet-baseline.mjs`](force-fleet-baseline.mjs) the scheduler runs as a subprocess when — and only when — a human forces it. This file is the human-facing record of what that is; there is no dispatch issue and no subagent.

## How to pull the lever

Run this repo's **Claudinite scheduler** workflow by hand (Actions → Claudinite scheduler → Run workflow) with `overrides`:

```
FORCE_TASKS=fleet-baseline
REPOS=Alpha Beta            ← optional: limit to these repos (bare name or owner/name, SPACE-separated); omit for every covered member
DRY_RUN=true                ← optional: report what would fire, fire nothing
INCLUDE_DORMANT=true        ← optional: dormant members are skipped by default — they stopped their own scheduler on purpose
```

Values are space-separated because the override bag splits `KEY=value` pairs on commas.

## What it does

Enumerate every repo under the configured owner over the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` PAT and, for each **covered, non-dormant** member, fire that member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` with `FORCE_TASKS=baselining` — the same button the owner would press in that repo's Actions tab, pressed across the fleet in one run. A forced run evaluates **only** the forced task (engine contract, #749), so each member does exactly one thing: baseline.

Nothing is baselined *here*, and nothing is written to any member — no commit, no issue, no comment. Each member converges its own mount, with its own token, under its own scheduler and delivery policy; if its converge needs an agent, that member's own executor runs it. The enforcer **dispatches**; the member **executes**. That is the whole trust model: no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access, and the one fleet credential is the PAT with Actions write.

Every repo under the owner lands in the run summary under exactly one state — fired, canon, out-of-scope, excluded, filtered-out, uncovered, dormant, or failed — so a fleet-wide force is never mistaken for fleet-wide coverage.

## What it deliberately does not do

**It does not wait.** A dispatch queues a run; what that run went on to do is each member's own story, told where members always tell it — a maintenance PR, a dispatch issue, a failure escalation in that repo. The retired workflow's *follow* half (watch every member to a terminal state, render a fleet report) is what forced the lever to be a standalone workflow with a 45-minute sleep; giving it up is what lets the lever ride the ordinary scheduler. If a member's forced run went wrong, that member says so in its own repo.

## Why a task and not a workflow (any more)

The standalone `fleet-baseline.yml` workflow (retired 2026-08-11, #749) lived in the enforcer's `.github/` — the one place the nightly converge can never push (#649), so every change to it crossed the fleet by the slow withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path. As a task, the lever ships with the ordinary vendor refresh like everything else, and the repo's vendored scheduler stays its **only** workflow. The typed `workflow_dispatch` inputs the old workflow offered are carried by the override bag above.

## Failure is loud

A member that could not be dispatched — a missing scheduler, a PAT without Actions write, a workflow GitHub disabled — is named in the summary under `failed`, and the sweep exits non-zero. The scheduler converges a `needs-human` issue for the task family, so a broken grant escalates rather than silently leaving part of the fleet unforced.

[Resource from github at repo://missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary/sha/349555f2a37dd360f3f99d4ab383f4acc0cb157c/contents/.github/workflows/claudinite-conformance.yml] # The Claudinite world sweep, on every pull request.
#
# Deliberately UNFILTERED — no `paths:` key. This repo is the canon's live
# canary: almost every change to it lands under `.claudinite/**`, which is
# exactly what a product-tree path filter would exclude. A filtered conformance
# workflow here would start no check at all on the changes that matter most.
#
# Two things depend on this workflow existing:
#
#   1. The maintenance PRs. `maintenance.delivery` is `auto-merge`, and GitHub's
#      auto-merge is a queue for CHECKS — with no check configured the arm
#      succeeds and the PR then waits forever. A canary whose nightly refresh
#      cannot land stops tracking the canon and stops being a canary.
#   2. The consumer-safety gate itself. The canon's canary-rehearsal converges
#      this repo against a candidate ref; the world sweep is the assertion that
#      answers whether a real member still works.
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not decoration: a branch pushed and a PR opened by the
# Actions GITHUB_TOKEN emit no `pull_request` event (GitHub's recursion guard),
# so baselining starts this workflow explicitly on its maintenance branch.
# Without the dispatch trigger it cannot, and the PR is back to having no checks.
#
# The WORK scope is deliberately absent: it judges a session's own change against
# that session's transcript and runs at the Stop hook, not in CI.
name: Claudinite conformance

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  conformance:
    name: Claudinite world sweep
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: '24'

      # The engine's always-vendored Node CLI, invoked as the standalone command
      # — never as a test file a language runner discovers.
      - name: Claudinite world scope
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs

**What I found:**

- Only two canon records carry a `materialize` op into `.github/workflows/`: `static-website/2026-07-31-static-site-vendoring` and `chrome-extension-release/2026-07-13-chrome-release-vendoring`.

- Its only two workflows are `claudinite-scheduler.yml` (the engine stub — delivered by the *already-exercised* `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` route) and `claudinite-conformance.yml`, which is hand-written per repo, not canon-owned (Sheepdog doesn't even have one; it folds the sweep into its own CI).

So editing an engine workflow and forcing an update would re-exercise the scheduler-workflow route that #649 already verified. The untested delta is specifically `applyMaterializations()` in `engine/migrations/registry.mjs:100` running with `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS=1` — a record's materialize reaching `write` → `withhold`. Nothing on the canary triggers that today, so a record has to exist first.

questions.question: Nothing the canary declares materializes a workflow, so there's no existing record to exercise. How should I create one?

options.label: One-off probe record (Recommended)
options.description: Add a dated record to `basics` (bump manifest 2→3) that materializes an inert probe workflow (workflow_dispatch only, no schedule/push) from a new canon template into `.github/workflows/`. Gate `appliesTo` on the repo declaring `local/canary`, so only the canary is touched — every other member evaluates it as a no-op. Records are dated one-offs that age out, so this is the shape the design already expects. Round two is then your 'random comment edit' to the template, to prove re-materialization stays current.

options.label: Vendor the conformance workflow
options.description: Make `.github/workflows/claudinite-conformance.yml` a canon-owned template with a standing vendoring record, the same pattern as static-site-vendoring. Genuinely useful — that file drifts freely today — but it's a fleet-wide standing feature, and members' copies differ meaningfully (the canary's is deliberately unfiltered), so canon would clobber per-repo choices. Bigger decision than a test.

options.label: Just edit the scheduler stub
options.description: Edit `engine/scheduler/stubs/claudinite-scheduler.yml`, merge, force the update. This is closest to what you literally asked for, but it drives `pendingSchedulerWorkflow`, not `applyMaterializations` — the route #649 already verified live. It would re-confirm the withhold lane end to end and leave the record-materialize case still untested.

# Fleet: get every member declaring the packs it is missing

**This task runs no agent.** It is `agent_model: none` with a parameterised `prework` ([`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs)), so the whole pass is deterministic code the scheduler runs as a subprocess. This file is the human-facing record of what that code does; there is no dispatch issue and no enforcer-side subagent. The *agentic* half of the job belongs to each member's own **adopt-requested-packs** task (grow_with_claudinite) — see "The fan-out model" below.

## Two first stages, one parameter set

The task is parameterised over the two ways a pack comes to be missing ([`params.mjs`](params.mjs) — no parameter has a default; both call sites say everything):

| run | parameters | first stage |
|---|---|---|
| weekly (scheduled) | `--scan-for-needed-packs=true --repos=all-covered-members`, on the `prework` line in [`task.mjs`](task.mjs) | the **scan** ([`scan-for-needed-packs.mjs`](scan-for-needed-packs.mjs)): fingerprint every covered member's tree against the canon corpus and *suspect* what its declaration does not carry |
| forced (hand-started) | the scheduler's override bag: `FORCE_TASKS=fleet-add-missing-packs`, `SCAN_FOR_NEEDED_PACKS=false`, `REPOS=Alpha Beta`, `ADD_PACKS=<ids>`, `PACK_CONFIG=<pack>.<key>=<v>`, `PACK_ANSWER=<pack>.<question>=<answer>` (values space-separated — the bag splits on commas) | the **force** ([`force-add-packs.mjs`](force-add-packs.mjs)): the owner names the packs, repos, config and interview answers — nothing is suspected, because it was decided |

A force **refuses itself entirely** — before any issue is written — on an unknown pack id, a repo that is not a covered member or is dormant, `all-covered-members` as a target, or **any adoption-interview question the overrides did not answer**: an answer is the owner's to give, never one this task may infer.

## The fan-out model

Both stages end the same way, per member with work ([`protocol.mjs`](protocol.mjs)):

1. **Converge one work-list issue in that member** under the `add-packs` label — `Add packs: requested for this repo` (a decision, carrying the exact declaration entries as JSON, config and answers included) or `Add packs: suspected from this repo’s shape` (a suspicion, carrying the evidence and the fingerprints the REST sweep could not decide).
2. **Fire that member's own scheduler** with `FORCE_TASKS=adopt-requested-packs`. A forced run evaluates only that task (engine contract, #749).

The member's task reads its own issue, its own executor confirms/adopts with the repo checked out, and one reviewed PR lands *there*. The enforcer **dispatches**; the member **executes**. Nothing here writes to any member's tree, and no agent anywhere needs cross-repo access — the one fleet credential is `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` (Contents read, Issues read/write, Actions read+write).

## Convergence

- A **requested** issue closes `completed` once the member's declaration carries everything its JSON block asks for — checked on every weekly visit, whichever run opened it.
- A **suspected** issue closes `completed` once the member declares the packs (or its shape stops suggesting them), and a `not planned` close is a standing decline the scan honours rather than re-suggesting weekly.
- A member with a still-open work list is **re-fired** on the weekly visit — the retry loop for a member whose earlier adoption run died.

## Failure is loud

A member that could not be swept is `unknown` — never "fitted" — and a member whose scheduler refused the dispatch (missing workflow, PAT without Actions write, workflow disabled) is a work list nobody will act on. Both are named in the summary and fail the run; the scheduler converges a `needs-human` issue for the task family.

Discovery is structural — any `packs//pack.mjs` is a pack, and that manifest is the pack's index: what it owns, the checks it runs in each scope, the skills it bundles. A pack's `README.md` is **optional** and carries only what the manifest cannot — provenance, design rationale, an index of its prose. A README that restates the manifest is duplication with a drift risk, and several had already drifted. ## Packs This table is the canon maintainer's view. marker: the `Release static site` orchestrator | 3 | 8 (+ RELEASE contract) | | [flutter](flutter/README.md) | pubspec.yaml | 0 | 0 (stub) | | [firebase](firebase/README.md) | `firebase.json` | 2 | rules / functions / deploy discipline | | [firebase-release](firebase-release/README.md) | declared (opt-in) | 0 | dev/prod split + App Check store gating | | [android](android/) | `AndroidManifest.xml` | 0 | stub | | [ios](ios/) | `ios/Runner/Info.plist` | 0 | stub | | [macos](macos/README.md) | `Package.swift` near root | 2 | bundle / TCC + Hardened Runtime / on-device speech / Developer ID + notarization / lifecycle | | [play-store-release](play-store-release/) | declared (opt-in) | 0 | stub | | [app-store-release](app-store-release/) | declared (opt-in) | 0 | stub | | [web-scraping](web-scraping/README.md) | declared (opt-in) | 0 | 27 (+ 1 skill: map-a-data-source) | | [research-project](research-project/README.md) | declared (class) | 0 | 56 (14 sections) | | [product-wiki](product-wiki/README.md) | declared (marker: `product-wiki/product-requirements/README.md`) | 7 | wiki growth discipline + weekly growth daily task | | [spec-driven-product](spec-driven-product/README.md) | declared (class) | 0 | 25 (8 sections) | | [executable-requirements](executable-requirements/README.md) | `dev/requirements/requirements.md` | 0 | framework standard (layout / gates / kinds) | ## Local packs — a project's own packs A consumer keeps its **project-specific** packs in its own tree at `.claudinite/local_packs//` — the same slots (prose `RULES.md`, `rules` checks, `skills`, scheduled `tasks/`, `questions`), authored and committed by the project, discovered and run by the same engine as these canon packs. `discoverPacks({ localRoot })` ([registry.mjs](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs)) scans this repo's `packs/` **and** the consumer's `local_packs/`; each pack is stamped with its own `dir` (prose and bundled skills resolve off it) and a `local` flag. A local pack: - is **declared by hand** in `.claudinite-checks.json` like any pack — never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` null) — by its **namespaced token `local_packs/`** (the canonical form; the engine's [`packEntryId`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) resolves it and the legacy bare id alike to the bare pack id, so the bare form keeps working while the fleet's update flows rewrite it), and its id must be unique (it may not shadow a canon id — the collision is a blocking `config` finding); - **bundles its skills** at `/skills//` (mounted from the tracked pack dir — the same one shape canon packs use); a bundled skill may carry `checks.mjs`, run when the pack is active; - rides the deployment plumbing every consumer already vendors: the sync hook preserves `.claudinite/local_packs/` across its dir swap and the `.gitignore` re-includes it. A local pack contributes **every** slot first-class: prose, checks, skills, **and scheduled tasks** — `tasks//task.mjs`, found by the repo's own scheduler in the same uniform scan that finds a canon pack's tasks ([../engine/scheduler/discover.mjs](../engine/scheduler/discover.mjs)), gated by the repo's declaration exactly like a canon pack's tasks. The canon home's own curation tasks ride this path. The canon-vs-local line is the portable-vs-project-specific split ([../extending.md](../extending.md)); a project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill, and the growth lifecycle treats `.claudinite/local_packs/` as the project's capture surface. ## Settings validity The `"packs"` list and the rest of `.claudinite-checks.json` are validated **when the file loads**, not by a conformance check: [`loadConfig`](../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs) reports malformed JSON and an unknown top-level property, and the runner adds an unknown *pack name* (it holds the registry). Each becomes a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as much a settings error as invalid JSON. A pack's `detect`/`marker` only **suspects** a pack is wanted; declaring it is the project's call, so a declared pack without its marker (or a marker without its declaration) is **not** flagged. ## Pack dependencies (`requires`) A pack states the packs it depends on in an optional `requires` field on its `pack.mjs` — a plain array of pack ids: a release pack builds on its coding pack (`chrome-extension-release` requires `chrome-extension`, `firebase-release` requires `firebase`) and a project-class pack leans on the framework that implements it (`spec-driven-product` requires `executable-requirements`). This is **not a check** — a pack can't be imported without its dependencies, so the resolution happens **when the declaration is written**, at bootstrap `--init` and the update backfill ([bootstrap.md](../bootstrap.md) Part 2): [`resolveDeclaredPacks`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) pulls each declared pack's transitive `requires` closure into `.claudinite-checks.json`. The prerequisite is materialized and visible in the file — droppable like every other entry, the same reason `basics` is written explicitly rather than defaulted — rather than resolved implicitly at run time. Declared ids keep their order; each pack's pulled-in dependencies land right after it. ## The manifest spec (`pack.mjs`) What a `pack.mjs` may and must carry is declared once, in [`engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs), and [`validateManifest`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs) is the only thing that judges a manifest against it. The **loader** runs it on every pack it imports, canon and local alike, so an incomplete or malformed declaration surfaces as a blocking `config` error at load — the same class as invalid JSON in `.claudinite-checks.json`, and for the same reason: a required manifest field is part of the pack contract, not a conformance opinion about a repo's content. A conformance *check* would have to be declared by a pack, run only when that pack is active, and re-derive the manifest by reading its source text — enforcing the shape of the system from inside one of its members. Reporting is not fatal: a pack whose declaration is incomplete still loads and still runs its checks. Silently disabling a repo's own rules is a worse failure than the one being reported. The field vocabulary is **closed** — an undeclared key is an error, so a typo (`rule:`, `skill:`) fails loudly instead of being ignored forever. ### `ruleRoutingGuidance` — what belongs here, and what does not ```js ruleRoutingGuidance: { belongs: 'workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls', excludes: 'git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack', }, ``` Both sides are required and each is capped at **20 words**. The cap is a session-context budget, not a style rule: [`inject-pack-prose`](../engine/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.mjs) emits the whole set as a **routing table at session start**, one row per pack, so a session deciding where a rule, doc, skill or check goes reads the answer instead of guessing. Guess-by-default lands everything in `basics` — that is the failure this field exists to stop. Write `excludes` to **name the pack that owns the other side** wherever one exists (`— that is chrome-extension-release`), so the table routes rather than merely refuses. A boundary that is **true of every pack carries no routing information** and wastes the row: "anything portable belongs in the canon" is the local-pack rule restated, not this local pack's edge. State what separates a pack from its **nearest neighbours** — the packs a reader would actually confuse it with. Sibling packs that split a domain (a technology pack and its `-release` pack, `basics` and `git-github`) are where the pair earns its keep, and their two declarations should agree on where the line falls. "No pack fits" is a real answer — it means a new pack, or the project's own `local_packs/` — never the baseline as a fallback. The table is emitted for every pack **discovered**, active or not: a consumer holds only the packs it vendored, so the discovered set is already what it can route into, and in the canon every pack is a legitimate destination. Local packs declare it on the same terms. ### `worldRules` / `workRules` — a rule's scope is its placement A pack declares its checks in two lists, and **which list a rule sits in is what makes it world- or work-scoped**: `worldRules` audit repo state ([`check_the_world`](../engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs)), `workRules` judge the change and session in front of you ([`check_the_work`](../engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs)). The loader flattens both into the single `rules` array the runners walk, stamping each rule's scope from the list it came from — one derivation, nothing downstream re-decides it. A rule module that carries its own `scope` field is a second source for the same fact, free to contradict the manifest a reader trusts, so the spec rejects it. A skill's own `checks.mjs` sits outside this partition (it is a skill's content, not a manifest list) and still declares `scope` on the rule itself. ### `skills` — the bundle, declared A pack's skills live in its own tree — `/skills//SKILL.md`, one owning pack per skill (#385) — and the manifest **names them**: `skills: ['merge-to-main', ...]`. The spec holds the declaration and the tree to each other in **both directions**: an undeclared directory is a skill nothing announces, and a declared name with no directory is a manifest that lies. What each skill covers stays in its own `SKILL.md` frontmatter, the description the harness triggers on — the manifest carries the membership, not a second copy of the summary. The SessionStart hook [`../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`](../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs) mounts the **union over the active packs' bundles** (same activation as prose/checks/env) as session-generated `.claude/skills/` symlinks — nothing committed, and a self-ignoring `.claude/skills/.gitignore` keeps them out of git status. A skill rides its pack everywhere the pack goes: the vendor set, the mounts, the sweep (its `checks.mjs` runs when the pack is active). The baseline activities every project has (`merge-to-main`, `writing-tests`, `bug-investigation`, …) ride the `basics` pack's bundle; move a skill's directory to a narrower pack when it stops being a baseline activity. ## Pack badge (`badge`)

A local pack: - is **declared by hand** in `.claudinite-checks.json` like any pack — never fingerprinted or seeded (`detect`/`marker` null) — by its **namespaced token `local_packs/`** (the canonical form; the engine's [`packEntryId`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) resolves it and the legacy bare id alike to the bare pack id, so the bare form keeps working while the fleet's update flows rewrite it), and its id must be unique (it may not shadow a canon id — the collision is a blocking `config` finding); - **bundles its skills** at `/skills//` (mounted from the tracked pack dir — the same one shape canon packs use); a bundled skill may carry `checks.mjs`, run when the pack is active; - rides the deployment plumbing every consumer already vendors: the sync hook preserves `.claudinite/local_packs/` across its dir swap and the `.gitignore` re-includes it. The canon-vs-local line is the portable-vs-project-specific split ([../extending.md](../extending.md)); a project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill, and the growth lifecycle treats `.claudinite/local_packs/` as the project's capture surface. ## Settings validity The `"packs"` list and the rest of `.claudinite-checks.json` are validated **when the file loads**, not by a conformance check: [`loadConfig`](../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs) reports malformed JSON and an unknown top-level property, and the runner adds an unknown *pack name* (it holds the registry). Each becomes a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as much a settings error as invalid JSON. A pack's `detect`/`marker` only **suspects** a pack is wanted; declaring it is the project's call, so a declared pack without its marker (or a marker without its declaration) is **not** flagged. ## Pack dependencies (`requires`) A pack states the packs it depends on in an optional `requires` field on its `pack.mjs` — a plain array of pack ids: a release pack builds on its coding pack (`chrome-extension-release` requires `chrome-extension`, `firebase-release` requires `firebase`) and a project-class pack leans on the framework that implements it (`spec-driven-product` requires `executable-requirements`). This is **not a check** — a pack can't be imported without its dependencies, so the resolution happens **when the declaration is written**, at bootstrap `--init` and the update backfill ([bootstrap.md](../bootstrap.md) Part 2): [`resolveDeclaredPacks`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) pulls each declared pack's transitive `requires` closure into `.claudinite-checks.json`. The prerequisite is materialized and visible in the file — droppable like every other entry, the same reason `basics` is written explicitly rather than defaulted — rather than resolved implicitly at run time. Declared ids keep their order; each pack's pulled-in dependencies land right after it. ## The manifest spec (`pack.mjs`) What a `pack.mjs` may and must carry is declared once, in [`engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs), and [`validateManifest`](../engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs) is the only thing that judges a manifest against it. The **loader** runs it on every pack it imports, canon and local alike, so an incomplete or malformed declaration surfaces as a blocking `config` error at load — the same class as invalid JSON in `.claudinite-checks.json`, and for the same reason: a required manifest field is part of the pack contract, not a conformance opinion about a repo's content. A conformance *check* would have to be declared by a pack, run only when that pack is active, and re-derive the manifest by reading its source text — enforcing the shape of the system from inside one of its members. Reporting is not fatal: a pack whose declaration is incomplete still loads and still runs its checks. Silently disabling a repo's own rules is a worse failure than the one being reported. The field vocabulary is **closed** — an undeclared key is an error, so a typo (`rule:`, `skill:`) fails loudly instead of being ignored forever. ### `ruleRoutingGuidance` — what belongs here, and what does not ```js ruleRoutingGuidance: { belongs: 'workflow YAML and Actions runner platform behaviour: triggers, secrets, permissions, scheduling, artifacts, reusable workflows and their pitfalls', excludes: 'git and GitHub command procedure — git-github; release pipeline content for one product — its release pack', }, ``` Both sides are required and each is capped at **20 words**. The cap is a session-context budget, not a style rule: [`inject-pack-prose`](../engine/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.mjs) emits the whole set as a **routing table at session start**, one row per pack, so a session deciding where a rule, doc, skill or check goes reads the answer instead of guessing. Guess-by-default lands everything in `basics` — that is the failure this field exists to stop. Write `excludes` to **name the pack that owns the other side** wherever one exists (`— that is chrome-extension-release`), so the table routes rather than merely refuses. A boundary that is **true of every pack carries no routing information** and wastes the row: "anything portable belongs in the canon" is the local-pack rule restated, not this local pack's edge. State what separates a pack from its **nearest neighbours** — the packs a reader would actually confuse it with. Sibling packs that split a domain (a technology pack and its `-release` pack, `basics` and `git-github`) are where the pair earns its keep, and their two declarations should agree on where the line falls. "No pack fits" is a real answer — it means a new pack, or the project's own `local_packs/` — never the baseline as a fallback. The table is emitted for every pack **discovered**, active or not: a consumer holds only the packs it vendored, so the discovered set is already what it can route into, and in the canon every pack is a legitimate destination. Local packs declare it on the same terms. ### `worldRules` / `workRules` — a rule's scope is its placement A pack declares its checks in two lists, and **which list a rule sits in is what makes it world- or work-scoped**: `worldRules` audit repo state ([`check_the_world`](../engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs)), `workRules` judge the change and session in front of you ([`check_the_work`](../engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs)). The loader flattens both into the single `rules` array the runners walk, stamping each rule's scope from the list it came from — one derivation, nothing downstream re-decides it. A rule module that carries its own `scope` field is a second source for the same fact, free to contradict the manifest a reader trusts, so the spec rejects it. A skill's own `checks.mjs` sits outside this partition (it is a skill's content, not a manifest list) and still declares `scope` on the rule itself. ### `skills` — the bundle, declared A pack's skills live in its own tree — `/skills//SKILL.md`, one owning pack per skill (#385) — and the manifest **names them**: `skills: ['merge-to-main', ...]`. The spec holds the declaration and the tree to each other in **both directions**: an undeclared directory is a skill nothing announces, and a declared name with no directory is a manifest that lies. What each skill covers stays in its own `SKILL.md` frontmatter, the description the harness triggers on — the manifest carries the membership, not a second copy of the summary. The SessionStart hook [`../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`](../engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs) mounts the **union over the active packs' bundles** (same activation as prose/checks/env) as session-generated `.claude/skills/` symlinks — nothing committed, and a self-ignoring `.claude/skills/.gitignore` keeps them out of git status. A skill rides its pack everywhere the pack goes: the vendor set, the mounts, the sweep (its `checks.mjs` runs when the pack is active). import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { join, dirname } from 'node:path';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { discoverPacks } from '../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs';
import { packRules } from '../engine/checks/run-active-pack-rules.mjs';

// packs/README.md's corpus tally quotes how many hardcoded checks the canon
// carries — a derived number that was hand-maintained and drifted badly (it
// read 41 while the runner listed 65, so the ratio it argues from was wrong by
// a third). The catalog is the single source of truth; this guard keeps the
// prose equal to it. `packRules` is the same assembly `--list` prints, so the
// tally can never disagree with the runner about what a rule is.
//
// Deliberately guards only the CHECK count. The prose-rule figures beside it
// are audit estimates from docs/conversion-inventory.md — nothing derives them,
// so the README marks them as a dated snapshot rather than pretending they are
// live, and no test can hold them honest.
const ROOT = join(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..');
const CATALOG = 'packs/README.md';
const TALLY = /\|\s*\*\*Hardcoded conformance checks\*\*\s*\|\s*\*\*(\d+)\*\*/;

test('the packs/ catalog tally equals the rule catalog the runner lists', async () => {
  const { packs } = await discoverPacks({ localRoot: ROOT });
  const actual = packRules(packs).length;

  const readme = readFileSync(join(ROOT, CATALOG), 'utf8');
  const m = TALLY.exec(readme);
  assert.ok(m, `${CATALOG} carries no parseable "Hardcoded conformance checks" tally — keep the bolded count in the corpus-tally table so this guard can read it`);
  assert.equal(
    Number(m[1]), actual,
    `${CATALOG} says ${m[1]} hardcoded checks; the catalog carries ${actual}. Update the tally (and the ratio it feeds) in the same change that adds or removes a rule.`
  );
});

import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { discoverPacks } from '../engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs';
import { ENGINE_VERSION } from '../engine/version.mjs';

// Every canon pack declares both version fields. The manifest spec cannot require
// them — a member's own local packs are repo-owned, carry no version, and nothing
// would carry a fix if the loader started rejecting them (DESIGN §8) — so the
// "canon packs are versioned" half is asserted here, over the canon tree, where it
// is the only tree the claim is about.
//
// Runs against the REAL pack set rather than a fixture: a fixture would keep proving
// that a manifest CAN carry a version while a newly added pack silently shipped
// without one. Discovered with no `localRoot`, so the home's own local packs — which
// are exactly the unversioned kind — stay out of scope.
test('every canon pack declares a version and the engine version it needs', async () => {
  const { packs } = await discoverPacks();
  assert.ok(packs.length > 20, `only ${packs.length} packs discovered — this test is asserting over the wrong tree`);

  for (const pack of packs) {
    assert.ok(Number.isInteger(pack.version) && pack.version > 0,
      `pack "${pack.id}" declares no version — add "version: 1" to packs/${pack.id}/pack.mjs`);
    assert.ok(Number.isInteger(pack.minEngineVersion) && pack.minEngineVersion > 0,
      `pack "${pack.id}" declares no minEngineVersion — add "minEngineVersion: 1" to packs/${pack.id}/pack.mjs`);
    // A pack that asks for an engine newer than the one it ships beside could never
    // apply anywhere: the canon is the newest engine that exists.
    assert.ok(pack.minEngineVersion <= ENGINE_VERSION,
      `pack "${pack.id}" requires engine version ${pack.minEngineVersion}, above the canon's own ${ENGINE_VERSION}`);
  }
});

input.content: canary-probe The canon's live proof that it can deliver a file into a member's `.github/workflows/`. ## Why it exists `.github/workflows/` is the one directory the nightly update can never push to. The update commits with the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, GitHub refuses that token under that path, and the refusal rejects the **whole ref** — so a single workflow write does not fail one file, it fails the entire converge and everything riding it. #649 is that problem. The answer is the **withhold lane** in [`updates/pack-update.mjs`](../../updates/pack-update.mjs): every write bound for `.github/workflows/` is diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, a path the Action token *can* push. It rides the maintenance PR as an ordinary added file — reviewable in the diff, recoverable if nothing else runs — and the update ends at `apply-stage` until a session holding an MCP credential moves it into place. That lane shipped with **one** exercised caller: the scheduler workflow's own convergence. A record's `materialize` goes through the same `write`, and had never run against a live member — the residual #649 was reopened for, and the last item left on #768. Proving it needs a record that materializes a workflow into a repo that really runs the update flow, and nothing in the corpus was one. This pack is that. ## What it ships | | | |---|---| | [`stubs/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml`](stubs/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml) | one inert workflow — `workflow_dispatch` only, no schedule, no push | | `seedOps` | seeds that file at **adoption**, written by the install flow and committed by the adopting session | | [`migrations/`](migrations/) | re-vendors the same path on later cycles, through the withhold lane | The two routes are the point, and their order is the point. Seeding is the easy half — the adopting session holds a credential the Action token does not, so nothing is being tested there. The record is the hard half, and because the file is already present by then, it has to *update* a workflow rather than create one — the exact shape a fleet-wide workflow fix would take. ## Who carries it `seededByDefault: false`, `detect: null`, `marker: null`. `--init` never seeds it, the fleet's pack scan never suspects it, and a repo carries it only because someone declared it by hand. The intended holder is **the canary** and nothing else: a probe belongs on the repo that exists to be converged against candidate refs and is disposable by construction. ## Reading the result The workflow's one step echoes a **revision marker**. "The file exists" stops being an assertion once the file has existed since adoption, so a delivery is watched by bumping that line in the template here and checking the member's copy against it. Current marker: **revision 1**.

input.body:
Comment class: other
The dispatch here was an owner instruction to test the last open item on #768 — "a record's `materialize` into `.github/workflows/` (#649's original case) shares the withhold path but has still never run live".

## The problem

`.github/workflows/` is the one path the nightly update cannot push to: it commits with the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, GitHub refuses that token under that path, and the refusal rejects the **whole ref** — so a single workflow write does not fail one file, it fails the entire converge and everything riding it.

The withhold lane in `updates/pack-update.mjs` answers that (#649): every write bound for `.github/workflows/` is diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, rides the maintenance PR as a reviewable added file, and the update parks at `apply-stage` until a session with an MCP credential moves it into place.

That lane shipped with exactly **one** exercised caller — `pendingSchedulerWorkflow`, the scheduler workflow's own convergence. A record's `materialize` goes through the same `write` in `applyMaterializations` and has never run against a live member.

It could not be run, either: the only two canon records that materialize into `.github/workflows/` belong to `static-website` and `chrome-extension-release`, and the canary declares neither. There was no vehicle.

## What this adds

`packs/canary-probe/` — one inert workflow, opt-in, intended for the canary and nowhere else.

- **Inert by design.** `workflow_dispatch` and nothing else: no schedule, no push, no `pull_request`. What is under test is whether the file *arrives*, not whether it runs, and a probe billing a member for Actions minutes on every push would be paying for an answer nobody asked for.
- **Carried by nobody unless asked.** `seededByDefault: false`, `detect: null`, `marker: null` — `--init` never seeds it and the fleet pack scan never suspects it.
- **Two delivery routes, in order.** `seedOps` puts the file in at adoption (written by the install flow, committed by the adopting session, which holds a credential the Action token is not — the easy half, and not what #649 doubted). The record that re-vendors it through the withhold lane lands at **version 2**.

## Why the version split is load-bearing

An install stamps the newest version and runs no records (`updates/install.mjs`), and `migrationApplies` is `want > have`. A record shipped in the version a repo adopts at is a record that repo can **never** reach — the same arithmetic behind the #823 correction on #768.

So the probe is adopted at version 1, which leaves a real gap for the update flow to close, and the record lands at version 2. It also means the record's job is to **update** a workflow that is already present, which is the shape a fleet-wide workflow fix would actually take.

## The plan this is step one of

1. **This PR** — land the pack at v1.
2. `fleet-add-missing-packs` from Sheepdog puts `canary-probe` on the canary; assert the workflow arrives in `.github/workflows/`.
3. Edit the workflow template here (bump its revision marker), land it at pack v2 with the `materialize` record and a hermetic test over the record's withhold.
4. Force an update on the canary via Sheepdog; assert the delivered copy carries the new marker — the live proof #649 asked for.

## Checks

Full suite green (1608 tests), world sweep 0 blocking. `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` regenerated by its own drift test; `packs/README.md` catalog row added.

# Adopt the packs this repo's work list asks for

You are here because prework found at least one open **`add-packs`** issue in **this** repo — the work list a fleet enforcer placed here (its sheepdog `fleet-add-missing-packs` task) before firing this scheduler. Your job: turn that work list into **one reviewed PR on this repo**. The whole of *how* is the [adopt-pack](../../skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) skill — declaring, the interview, re-vendoring, scaffolding, getting the checks green, landing. Don't re-derive it here.

## The work list

The open issues labelled `add-packs` in this repo ([`protocol.mjs`](protocol.mjs) is the contract). There are at most two, and the title says what each is:

| title | what it is | what you owe it |
|---|---|---|
| `Add packs: requested for this repo` | a **decision** — the fleet owner named the packs, and the issue's JSON block is the exact declaration entries to write, `config` and `answers` included (the answers are the owner's interview answers, already given) | adopt it verbatim (§2) — never re-litigate whether it was wanted |
| `Add packs: suspected from this repo’s shape` | a **suspicion** — the weekly fleet scan fingerprinted file shapes against packs this repo does not declare | confirm each pack first (§1), adopt what survives, decline the rest with a reason |

An empty work list never reaches you — prework requests no agent for one. If both issues are open, they are one adoption: one PR covers both.

## 1. Confirm a *suspicion* before acting on it

A fingerprint **suspects**; it does not prove. Per suspected pack:

- Read that pack's `README.md` and its `ruleRoutingGuidance` (in this repo's mount, `.claudinite/shared/packs/<id>/`). Does this repo's actual use match what the pack owns, or did the marker merely happen to be present? A `package.json` in a repo that ships no JavaScript is a fixture, not a Node project.
- Where the issue lists fingerprints under **Not decided from outside**, you can settle them exactly — you have the checkout the fleet's REST sweep did not. Use `localFits` from the enforcer-side task's `fingerprint-fit.mjs` (vendored in the canon clone adopt-pack's re-vendor step fetches) against a context built over this checkout.
- A pack you judge **not** wanted is a real answer: say which and why in a comment on the issue. If every suspected pack is declined, close the issue `not planned` — a standing answer the weekly scan honours rather than re-suggesting.

A suspected pack that asks interview questions the repo cannot answer from its own contents follows adopt-pack's unattended rule: never guess, finish what the question does not gate, and hand off in the open.

## 2. Adopt

Run **adopt-pack** for the confirmed and requested packs. Two things belong to you rather than the skill:

- **On a requested issue, merge the rendered entries verbatim** into `.claudinite-checks.json`'s `packs` — into an entry this repo already carries where one exists, never replacing a `config` this repo already chose. The `answers` are recorded answers; transcribe them, don't re-ask.
- **One PR for the whole work list**, and **link both ways**: the PR body names the issue(s), and you comment the PR link on each. The fleet's weekly sweep closes them on its own once the declaration carries the packs; your comment is what makes the intervening week legible.

## 3. Report

Close out on your dispatch issue as usual: the packs adopted with the PR link, the packs declined with the reason, and anything left for a human — an adoption blocked on an unanswerable interview question is exactly that, and naming it is the whole handoff.

## What you must not do

- **Never merge.** This task is ceilinged at `open-pr` and the executor enforces it in code (`verify-outcome.mjs`); merging fails the run.
- **Never declare a pack you did not confirm** (suspected) **or that was not requested**, and never guess an interview answer — see adopt-pack's rule. If you believe a *requested* entry is wrong, say so on the issue and leave it for a human; never quietly adopt something else in its place.

13-# serializes runs so a slow run and its successor never overlap.

The update commits with the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, GitHub refuses that token under that path, and the refusal rejects the **whole ref** — so a single workflow write does not fail one file, it fails the entire converge and everything riding it. #649 is that problem. The answer is the **withhold lane** in [`updates/pack-update.mjs`](../../updates/pack-update.mjs): every write bound for `.github/workflows/` is diverted to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, a path the Action token *can* push. It rides the maintenance PR as an ordinary added file — reviewable in the diff, recoverable if nothing else runs — and the update ends at `apply-stage` until a session holding an MCP credential moves it into place. That lane shipped with **one** exercised caller: the scheduler workflow's own convergence. git add -A && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
canary-probe v2: the record that materializes a workflow, and the tests for it

The first canon record whose `materialize` targets `.github/workflows/`, which is
the one branch of `applyMaterializations` that had never executed. The pack flow
sets CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS and routes the write to
`.claudinite/pending-workflows/`; every part of that shipped, but only the
scheduler workflow's own convergence had ever driven it, from the other side.

Version 2 is load-bearing, not bookkeeping. An install stamps the newest version
and runs no records, and `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, so a record shipped
at the version a repo adopts at can never reach it. The probe is adopted at 1
(seeded, nothing more); this lands at 2, so a member really has a gap — and the
record UPDATES a workflow already present, which is the shape a fleet-wide
workflow fix would take. The gate is the workflow's own `name:`, so it touches
only a repo carrying the probe and never the canon.

The template's revision marker moves 1 -> 2. "The file exists" stops being an
assertion once the file has existed since adoption, so the marker is what says
which route delivered the copy a member holds.

Two tests, both watched failing first:

- the record's materialize is WITHHELD, not written — destination untouched, the
  template staged byte for byte, apply stage needed, and the staging directory
  swept once delivered. Fails if the flow's workflow routing is removed.
- a caller that cannot deliver gets a reported SKIP, never a write. This is the
  latent half of #649: the flow announced the capability before it had the
  mechanism, so a record like this one would have been written into a tree the
  Action token was about to push, taking the whole converge down. Fails if the
  capability guard is removed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01DhDGKHnPEhZ7KFj6xL8gp8
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -1

**Where things stand:**

| step | state |
|---|---|
| 1. `canary-probe` v1 in canon | ✅ merged, `07994cb` (#829) |
| 2. Sheepdog force → canary | ✅ work-list #66 filed, dispatch #67 claimed, executor session running |
| 3. v2 + record + tests | ✅ committed on branch (`45c21cb`), **held back from `main`** |
| 4. Force update, assert delivery | pending |

**On step 3** — the two tests are the coverage the lane never had, and I watched each fail before trusting it:

- Removing the workflow routing in `updates/pack-update.mjs` (`write` no longer diverts to `withhold`) fails the record-withhold test and nothing else.
- Removing the capability guard in `applyMaterializations` fails the skip test and nothing else.

Comment class: other
Step 3 of the sequence set out in #829 — an owner instruction to test the last open item on #768, not a new requirement.

**Do not merge until the canary has adopted `canary-probe` at version 1.** The adopting session installs from a fresh canon clone and stamps the newest version it finds. With v2 on `main` it would stamp `canary-probe: 2`, `migrationApplies` (`want > have`) would be false forever, and the record could never run — closing the gap this PR exists to open. Tracking the canary's adoption PR; this merges after it lands.

## The record

`packs/canary-probe/migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/` — the first canon record whose `materialize` targets `.github/workflows/`.

That is the one branch of `applyMaterializations` (`engine/migrations/registry.mjs:100`) that had never executed. The pack update flow sets `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS` and routes the write to `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`; every part of that shipped, but the only caller that ever drove it was `pendingSchedulerWorkflow`, reaching the same `write` from the other side.

Standing, not transitional — `legacyPresent` is false by construction. Its job is to keep the vendored copy equal to the pack's template, the same shape and the same reason as `static-website`'s `static-site-vendoring`. The gate is the workflow's own `name:`, so it touches only a repo carrying the probe, and never the canon (which holds the template under `packs/` and no copy in its own `.github/workflows/`).

## The revision marker moves 1 → 2

"The file exists" stops being an assertion once the file has existed since adoption. The marker is what says *which route* delivered the copy a member holds: `revision 1` is the seed, `revision 2` is the record, through the withhold lane.

## The tests

Neither existed. `engine-tests/pack-update.test.mjs` covered the scheduler-workflow route and nothing else. Both were watched failing before being trusted:

| test | fails when |
|---|---|
| a **record**'s materialize is withheld, not written | the workflow routing is removed from `write` in `updates/pack-update.mjs` |
| a caller that cannot deliver gets a reported **skip** | the capability guard is removed from `applyMaterializations` |

Each mutation fails only its own test — no overlap, so neither is riding on the other's coverage.

The second is the latent half of #649, and worth naming: the pack flow *announced* `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS` before the mechanism existed. The first record to materialize a workflow would have been written into a tree the Action token was about to push, and GitHub's refusal rejects the whole ref — failing every member's converge, not just that file. It stayed latent only because no record had ever declared such a materialization. This PR adds the first one, so the branch is now guarded from both sides.

## Checks

`engine-tests/pack-update.test.mjs` 20/20, migrations + pack-version + directory + badge suites 45/45, world sweep 0 blocking.

## What this is step 3 of

1. ✅ #829 — the pack at v1.
2. ✅ Sheepdog `fleet-add-missing-packs` → canary work-list #66, dispatch #67 claimed.
3. **This PR** — v2, the record, the tests. Held.
4. Force an update on the canary via Sheepdog; assert the staged file appears in `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`, the update parks at `apply-stage`, and the delivered copy reads `revision 2`.

Step 4's assertion is the live proof #649 was reopened for.

My own scheduled check-in, not an owner comment.

**Assertions so far, honestly:**

| # | assertion | result |
|---|---|---|
| a | PR adds `.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml`, `.github/workflows/` untouched | ✅ 31 files, staging path added, target absent |
| — | staged copy is the new template | ✅ `revision 2` |

| — | session moves it byte-for-byte, staging swept | ✅ executor pushed `a467a81` at 17:08 |
| c | `main` reads `revision 2` | ❌ **not yet** — still revision 1 |

**The thing that didn't behave as I'd described it.** I said step 4 would end with the file on `main`. It didn't, and the reason isn't a fault in the withhold lane — it's that the lane's *last* step has an owner nobody names clearly:

`packs/basics/tasks/update/worker.mjs:227` merges only when `terminal.action === 'merge'`. The `apply-stage` terminal isn't that, so auto-merge is never armed, and the PR body says as much. The task file then tells the session to "let the PR land per this repo's delivery setting" — but under `auto-merge` nothing arms it, so the session correctly pushed and stopped. Delivery falls to the *next* cycle's `disposeOpenPull`, which merges a green incumbent.

So the design does converge, one cycle later. On a daily `update` that's a ~24h gap between a workflow being staged and reaching `.github/workflows/`. That's the same shape as the correction already recorded on #768 ("`update` is a daily task, not hourly"), now with a concrete instance. Whether that latency is acceptable or the apply stage should arm on its way out is a design call I'll put to you rather than decide.

I've forced the second cycle so the assertion completes now instead of tomorrow. Check-in armed; I'll report the final state and then write up #649 and #768.

Comment class: other
Reporting the result of the live verification this issue asked for; no new requirement.

## The reopen condition did not fire

> Reopen if a record's materialization behaves differently from the scheduler-workflow path — both go through the same `write`, but only the latter has been exercised against a live member.

It does not behave differently. Run end to end on the canary, 2026-08-14.

## What was run

Nothing in the corpus materialized a workflow into a repo the canary declares — the only two such records belong to `static-website` and `chrome-extension-release`. So the vehicle had to be built: **`canary-probe`** (#829, #830), an opt-in pack shipping one inert workflow, adopted at pack version 1 (seeded via `seedOps`) so that the record at version 2 had a real gap to close.

The version split matters and is worth recording: an install stamps the newest version and runs no records, and `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, so a record shipped at the version a repo adopts at can never reach it. Adopting at 1 and landing the record at 2 is what made the record reachable at all — and it made the record **update** a workflow already present, which is the shape a real fleet-wide workflow fix would take, rather than the easier create-from-nothing case.

## Observed, in order

| stage | evidence |
|---|---|
| adoption seeds the file | canary #68 — `.github/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml` at `revision 1`, committed by the adopting session, stamped `canary-probe: 1` |
| record materializes, withheld | canary #69 — 31 files changed; `.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml` **added**, `.github/workflows/` **absent from the entire diff** |
| staged content is the new template | staged blob = `revision 2` |
| update parks at `apply-stage` | dispatch #70, `escalation:apply-stage`, "1 withheld workflow file(s)" |
| record recorded as applied | `packVersions.canary-probe` 1 → 2 |
| session delivers | executor moved it byte-for-byte, pushed `a467a81`, staging swept |
| lands on `main` | `.github/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml` = blob `b6296b3`, `revision 2` — **the same blob SHA the staging directory held**, so byte-for-byte is measured, not asserted |
| lane closes | `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` gone from `main`; next cycle: no branch, no PR, no dispatch |

The Action token never touched `.github/workflows/`, and a session credential closed the lane. That is the whole of what this issue doubted.

## Also closed: the latent half

The other branch of `applyMaterializations` — a caller that has **not** announced `CLAUDINITE_CAN_WITHHOLD_WORKFLOWS` must report a skip rather than write — had also never executed, for the same reason: no record declared such a materialization. This issue's own text called that out ("the announcement predated the mechanism … Latent only because no record has yet declared such a materialization"). `canary-probe` is now that record, so both branches are exercised and both are pinned by tests in `engine-tests/pack-update.test.mjs`, each watched failing under a targeted mutation before being trusted.

## One thing that did not behave as I expected

Delivery took **two** cycles, not one, and the reason is not in the withhold lane.

`packs/basics/tasks/update/worker.mjs:227` merges only when `terminal.action === 'merge'`. The `apply-stage` terminal is not that, so auto-merge is never armed — the PR body says so itself ("before anything merges"). §5 of `packs/basics/tasks/update/task.md` then tells the session to "push to the branch and let the PR land per this repo's delivery setting", but under `auto-merge` nothing has armed it, so the session correctly pushes and stops. The PR is delivered by the *next* cycle's `disposeOpenPull`, which merged it here once forced.

So the lane converges, one cycle late. On a daily `update` that is a ~24h gap between a workflow being staged and reaching `.github/workflows/` — the concrete instance of the "`update` is a daily task, not hourly" correction already recorded on #768. Whether the apply stage should arm on its way out, or that latency is acceptable, is a design call and not something this verification settles.

# Update — the apply stage

The deterministic half already ran. Preprocessing converged this repo's mount to the
canon's current engine and pack versions, ran the version-ranged migrations, gated the
result on the converged tree's own `selftest --strict`, and opened the update PR. The
dispatch issue names the branch and says which packs moved.

**You are here for one of two reasons**, and the issue says which:

- **Withheld workflow files** — content the deterministic half already decided but its
  Action token is refused for. Nothing here needs judgment; you are the credential.
- **A pack's updated rules have met content this repo authored** and the canon has never
  seen. This is the half that needs judgment, and it is all of the judgment there is.

## 1. Read why you are here

The dispatch issue's **Why the agent is here** section names the terminal and the packs
whose versions moved. That is binding scope — do not widen it.

## 2. Deliver any withheld workflow files

GitHub never lets an Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` write under `.github/workflows/`, and the
refusal rejects the whole push — so the update flow stages that content instead of
committing it where it belongs. Anything staged is already on the branch, already in the
PR's diff, and already correct.

If `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` has files in it, then for each one:

- Move it to `.github/workflows/` under the same name — **byte for byte**.
- Delete the staged copy.

Do not reformat it, do not reorder it, do not reconcile it against what the file used to
say. It is a converged artifact, not a draft: the cron minute is a hash of this repo's
full name and the `env:` block is the union of every scheduled task's `required_secrets`,
so an "improvement" here silently changes when this repo runs or which secrets its tasks
can see. A staged file that looks wrong is a `needs-human` end (§5), reported with what
looked wrong — that is a canon bug, and editing it here would hide it while leaving every
other member broken.

An empty or absent `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` means there is nothing owed. Do not
create it, and never move a file INTO it.

## 3. Apply the new rules

Only if the issue's reason names a migration record — it names them by path, e.g.
`packs/basics/migrations/2026-08-13-something`. **Read that record** at
`.claudinite/shared/<path>/migration.mjs`: its `applyStage.instructions` say what its
author wanted done, in their words, and are the specific half of this section. The
record is on the branch you were given because the update that raised it vendored it
there. A record the issue names but the branch does not carry is a `needs-human` end
(§5) — guessing at what its author wanted is worse than reporting it missing.

Then, on that branch:

- Bring this repo's own content in line with the updated pack rules, and repair the
  tests those rules break.
- Nothing outside that scope. No new features, no unrelated tidy-ups, no rewriting a
  member-authored local pack beyond what the new rules require.

## 4. Verify the executor routine

# Update — the apply stage

The deterministic half already ran. Preprocessing converged this repo's mount to the
canon's current engine and pack versions, ran the version-ranged migrations, gated the
result on the converged tree's own `selftest --strict`, and opened the update PR. The
dispatch issue names the branch and says which packs moved.

**You are here for one of two reasons**, and the issue says which:

- **Withheld workflow files** — content the deterministic half already decided but its
  Action token is refused for. Nothing here needs judgment; you are the credential.
- **A pack's updated rules have met content this repo authored** and the canon has never
  seen. This is the half that needs judgment, and it is all of the judgment there is.

## 1. Read why you are here

The dispatch issue's **Why the agent is here** section names the terminal and the packs
whose versions moved. That is binding scope — do not widen it.

## 2. Deliver any withheld workflow files

GitHub never lets an Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` write under `.github/workflows/`, and the
refusal rejects the whole push — so the update flow stages that content instead of
committing it where it belongs. Anything staged is already on the branch, already in the
PR's diff, and already correct.

If `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` has files in it, then for each one:

- Move it to `.github/workflows/` under the same name — **byte for byte**.
- Delete the staged copy.

Do not reformat it, do not reorder it, do not reconcile it against what the file used to
say. It is a converged artifact, not a draft: the cron minute is a hash of this repo's
full name and the `env:` block is the union of every scheduled task's `required_secrets`,
so an "improvement" here silently changes when this repo runs or which secrets its tasks
can see. A staged file that looks wrong is a `needs-human` end (§5), reported with what
looked wrong — that is a canon bug, and editing it here would hide it while leaving every
other member broken.

An empty or absent `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` means there is nothing owed. Do not
create it, and never move a file INTO it.

## 3. Apply the new rules

Only if the issue's reason names a migration record — it names them by path, e.g.
`packs/basics/migrations/2026-08-13-something`. **Read that record** at
`.claudinite/shared/<path>/migration.mjs`: its `applyStage.instructions` say what its
author wanted done, in their words, and are the specific half of this section. The
record is on the branch you were given because the update that raised it vendored it
there. A record the issue names but the branch does not carry is a `needs-human` end
(§5) — guessing at what its author wanted is worse than reporting it missing.

Then, on that branch:

- Bring this repo's own content in line with the updated pack rules, and repair the
  tests those rules break.
- Nothing outside that scope. No new features, no unrelated tidy-ups, no rewriting a
  member-authored local pack beyond what the new rules require.

## 4. Verify the executor routine

The one check no Action can make. This repo's executor routine fires on the
`ready-for-agent` label, and it is not a GitHub artifact — only a session can see it.
Confirm it exists and that its prompt points at the mounted executor instructions
(`.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/executor.md`). Report what you found either way.

## 5. End green, or end at `needs-human`

Run this repo's checks. Green: push to the branch and let the PR land per this repo's
delivery setting. Not green, or a repair you are not sure of: leave the PR open, label
it `needs-human`, and say in one comment what is unresolved. A withheld workflow you did
not deliver is "not green" — it stays owed, and the next cycle will stage it again.

Every non-green end looks the same here, and that is the point — a repair nobody
verified is not a smaller problem than a red check, it is the same problem with less
evidence.
